context: linear network · pipe laying by zone, pump station & controllers, finished ahead of planting

brief.intro: New to this project type? An irrigation network delivers water — usually treated sewage effluent (TSE) — to landscaped areas, street trees and parks. A storage tank and pump station feed a ring of main lines; from them, valve-controlled laterals feed drip lines, bubblers and sprinklers in each planting zone, all switched by a central controller. The pipes are small and shallow, so laying is fast. What governs the programme is the order of work with the landscape and the roads: sleeves under roads and paving must go in before the surfacing, the network must be tested and running before the first plants arrive, and planting itself depends on the season.

must_get_right: Install every road and paving sleeve before the road base and paving — a missed sleeve means cutting a finished road.
The network must be pressure-tested, flushed and operating before plants are delivered; plants cannot wait for water.
Tie the planting dates to the season and work backwards: soil, irrigation and testing must all finish before that date.
Power to the pump station and the TSE source connection are outside dependencies — track both as milestones.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by irrigation zone (matching the landscape zones) with the pump station and main lines as common works, so each zone can be read as ready for planting or not.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar. Planting windows are marked by season; in hot climates summer planting is avoided or planned with reduced survival allowance.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Sleeves precede road base and paving. Main lines and the pump station must be tested before any zone is commissioned. In each zone: laterals → flush → emitters → zone test → planting. The critical path normally runs through the pump station (tank, pumps, power) or through the zone released last by other trades.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The TSE source or tank filling point is available; permanent power reaches the pump station on the assumed date; road and hardscape contractors give access to each zone in the planned order; final soil levels are complete before laterals.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Before lateral works in the first zone

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Irrigation follows the civil and hardscape trades into each area and is squeezed if they are late. Shallow pipes are easily damaged by later trades — protection and re-testing must be allowed for.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: missed sleeves, late power or water source, damage by other trades after testing, late zone release, and planting pushed into the wrong season. Contingency is held before the planting start of the first and last zones.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by irrigation zone; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the pipe, valve and emitter crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
